newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: EBRD may shift focus as East Europe changes.
newsitem.headline: EBRD may shift focus as East Europe changes.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), launched to help to transform former Soviet bloc economies, is facing calls for its own change as East European states develop at different rates.

Some of the region's most advanced economies want the bank, which holds its annual meeting in London next week, to become more of a traditional commercial lender to the private sector, while others still seek investment to help governments to change the structure of their economies.
"The nature of what they do has certainly changed and the focus has shifted from initial countries to a new group," said Philip Poole, ING Barings director of emerging Europe research.
"These markets are all at different stages of development and the ones that moved more quickly are less dependent on international financial institution funding," he said.
Poole said the bank's focus should shift towards Russia and other members of the Commonwealth of Independent States, which groups former Soviet republics except the Baltic states.
For the most developed economies, the EBRD meeting will be a shop window to show off successes. Less advanced economies will be keen to get their hands on more EBRD cash.

The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are members of the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) which groups richer industrialised countries, and are likely candidates for the next wave of European Union membership.
"We would like to see the EBRD more and more as a commercial bank," said Pavel Stapanek, director general of the Czech Finance Ministry.
"It is a question of cultivation of the bank in line with the development of our part of the world," he added.
He said the bank should be increasingly involved in private sector projects and added: "There is no reason for it (the EBRD) to expand any further in the Czech Republic."
A basic aim of the London-based bank is to promote the private sector in building market economies in the post-communist countries.

Polish Finance Minister Marek Belka said the EBRD meeting was a chance to promote its economic achievements and encourage "First of all this is an opportunity to present Poland at an international forum, present the state of our economy and encourage further investments," he told public radio.
Around 40 percent of EBRD commitments in Poland are in equity investments, about twice the bank's overall average.

EBRD president Jacques de Larosiere, who visited Warsaw last month, said this was showed the bank's confidence in the Polish economy. The bank was ready to help in privatising banks and other financial institutions, he said.
Slovenia, which has one of the region's strongest economies, also hopes to encourage investment.

"We expect the EBRD to invest mainly in the private sector this year and to participate in ecological projects and in projects that promote regional development," Andrej Kavcic, government consultant, told Reuters.
But Bulgaria, whose economy is in crisis, hopes radical reforms pledged by its interim cabinet will boost EBRD investment and win help with privatisation.

"With the latest news of approved international funding, Bulgarian investment prospects have improved and there are chances of speeding up EBRD projects planned for this year," central bank deputy governor Plamen Ilchev told Reuters.
Ilchev hopes to attract funds from portfolio investors into Bulgarian external and domestic debt instruments, and the bank's participation in sell-offs of major state firms.

The bank revised its funding strategy for Bulgaria last year after delayed reforms deterred development of the private sector. Bulgaria has yet to meet a 60/40 private/public portfolio requirement which is due in June 1997.
Slovak Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik is expected to discuss the sale of the EBRD's stake in oil refiner Slovnaft to the National Property Fund -- the state privatisation agency.
The EBRD took a 10.5 percent stake in Slovnaft in 1995 when it bought half the refiner's $113 million issue of global depositary receipts, which flopped on international markets.

The bank effectively paid the 1,000 crowns ($32.09) per share face value. But the NPF later sold an additional 39 percent of Slovnaft to a management-led consortium called Slovintegra at an implied prices of just 156 crowns per share.
The bank later said it would do business in Slovakia only through credit activities rather than ownership participation.
